name: Conjunctions
summary: Although, because, whereas and avoiding doubled linkers.

paragraphs: Conjunctions are the words that join ideas together: and, but, because, although, so, whereas. They show the reader how two ideas are related: whether one causes the other, contrasts with it or simply adds to it. Without them, writing feels like a list of separate statements.

Many learners know these words well but use two of them where English needs only one, or follow a linking word with the wrong grammar. For example, despite needs a noun, but although needs a full clause. This page sorts out the most common linking words and the grammar that follows each one.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: One linker per link: although or but, because or so, never both. Then check what follows: a clause or a noun?

paragraphs: Linking ideas clearly is central to the Coherence and Cohesion criterion, and using conjunctions accurately also supports your grammar score. A sentence like Although it is expensive, but many people buy it is a very common error, and examiners recognize it immediately.
Using a variety of linkers correctly, such as whereas, despite and as a result, shows control of complex sentences, which is part of reaching the higher bands.
The most useful way to learn linking words is by their job and by the grammar that follows them. Some join two full clauses, some come before a noun phrase, and some start a new sentence.

rows: in addition to, as well as

paragraphs: Although and even though already show contrast, so the second half of the sentence must not start with but. Using both is like saying the same thing twice. Choose one: either Although…, … or …, but ….
This is probably the single most common conjunction error in IELTS essays.

items.text: Although cars are convenient, but they cause pollution.
Although cars are convenient, they cause pollution.
Cars are convenient, but they cause pollution.

paragraphs: The same idea applies to cause and result. Because introduces the reason, and so introduces the result, so you only need one of them in a sentence.
Choose because when you want to focus on the reason, and so when you want to focus on the result.

items.text: Because the city is crowded, so many people move to the suburbs.
Because the city is crowded, many people move to the suburbs.
The city is crowded, so many people move to the suburbs.

sections.title: Rule 3: Despite and in spite of + noun or -ing
sections.label: Rule 3: Despite and in spite of + noun or -ing

paragraphs: Despite and in spite of have the same meaning as although, but different grammar. They are prepositions, so they must be followed by a noun, a noun phrase or an -ing form, not a full clause with a subject and verb.
Also remember: despite never takes of, while in spite of always does.

rows: Despite the high cost, … / Although it is expensive, …
Despite the rain, … / In spite of the rain, …
Despite working hard, … / Despite the fact that he worked hard, …

paragraphs: Because joins a full clause: because prices rose. Because of and due to come before a noun phrase: because of the price rise, due to rising prices.
Mixing them up, as in because of prices rose, is a common error. Ask yourself: does a subject and verb follow? If yes, use because.

items.text: Many shops closed because of rents increased.
Many shops closed because rents increased.
Many shops closed because of rising rents.

sections.title: Rule 5: However is not a conjunction
sections.label: Rule 5: However is not a conjunction

paragraphs: However looks like but, but it works differently. But joins two clauses in one sentence. However usually starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon) and is followed by a comma.
Using however with only commas to join two clauses creates a comma splice, which is a punctuation error (see the Comma Splices unit).

items.text: Cars are useful, however they cause pollution.
Cars are useful. However, they cause pollution.
Cars are useful; however, they cause pollution.
Cars are useful, but they cause pollution.

sections.title: Rule 6: Whereas and while for comparisons
sections.label: Rule 6: Whereas and while for comparisons

paragraphs: Whereas and while compare two different facts directly, which makes them very useful in Task 1 and in Task 2 comparisons. They join two full clauses in one sentence.
On the other hand cannot do this job in the middle of a sentence. It normally starts a new sentence and introduces a contrasting point.

items.text: Sales rose in City A, whereas they fell in City B.
While some people prefer cities, others choose rural life.
Sales rose in City A, on the other hand they fell in City B.
Sales rose in City A. On the other hand, they fell in City B.

paragraphs: Unless means if… not. Because the negative meaning is already inside unless, the verb after it should normally be positive.
Writing unless… not creates a double negative and usually reverses the meaning you intended.

items.text: Unless the government does not act, pollution will increase.
Unless the government acts, pollution will increase.
If the government does not act, pollution will increase.

sections.title: Rule 8: One linker at a time
sections.label: Rule 8: One linker at a time

paragraphs: Words like therefore, moreover, in addition and as a result connect the meaning of two sentences, but they do not join them grammatically. They usually start a new sentence and are followed by a comma.
Also avoid stacking two linkers together, such as and moreover or but however. One clear linker is enough.

items.text: Fuel prices rose, therefore many people bought smaller cars.
Fuel prices rose. Therefore, many people bought smaller cars.
But however, some people disagree.
However, some people disagree.

paragraphs: Here is how linking words appear in real IELTS writing.

rows: Coal use fell, whereas gas use rose.
Despite a fall in 2015, sales recovered.
Although technology helps students, it can be distracting.
Many people drive because public transport is poor.
Unless governments act, the problem will grow.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common linking mistakes in IELTS essays.

rows: Unless people… / If people do not…

paragraphs: Use this routine on every linking word in your final check.

steps: Check for doubled linkers: although… but, because… so.
Check what follows: a full clause after although, because and whereas; a noun or -ing after despite, because of and due to.

furtherStudy.title: British Council LearnEnglish: Contrasting Ideas
furtherStudy.description: Although, despite, however and more, with exercises.

cards.front: Although the test was hard, ____ most students passed.
cards.why: Although already shows contrast, so we must not add but.

cards.front: Many people use cars ____ the high cost of fuel.
cards.why: A noun phrase follows (the high cost), so we need despite, not although.

cards.front: The flight was delayed ____ the storm.
cards.why: A noun follows (the storm), so we use because of.

cards.front: ____ it was raining, the match continued.
cards.why: A full clause follows (it was raining), so we need although.

cards.front: Unless you ____, you will miss the bus.
cards.why: Unless already means if not, so the verb after it is positive.

cards.front: Prices rose in the city, ____ they fell in rural areas.
cards.why: We are comparing two clauses, so we use whereas.

cards.front: The rent was too high. ____, we moved to a smaller flat.
cards.why: Therefore starts a new sentence and shows a result. Because cannot be used this way.

cards.front: ____ of the cost, many families buy new phones every year.
cards.why: In spite always takes of. Despite never does.

cards.front: Because the roads were flooded, ____ schools were closed.
cards.why: Because already shows the reason, so we must not add so.

cards.front: She stayed at home ____ she was ill.
cards.why: A full clause follows (she was ill), so we use because. Due to needs a noun.
